Supersaturation of English words into the German language is, to my view, a legitimate problem, though not one without precedent: until two centuries ago, German suffered from a glut of French and Latin words. If it was not for the conscious effort of German authors and authorities to produce native substitutes, the modern German language might more closely resemble the English in this sense.

Often there is already a sound German equivalent that is not commonly used, but presents its own meaning; I use Rechner (related to the English word reckon) in place of Computer. Even more bewildering is that this occurs even to things that existed before America or England existed as countries: the native Säugling (suckler) or Kleinkind (small child) have given way to Baby, which we of course pluralise as Babys. I keep saved to my computer a dictionary of English loans and native equivalents for this purpose.

English words, due to the vowel shifts and general slurring, do not assimilate very well into Continental languages; even French words have converted themselves relatively seamlessly, such that bureau became the phonetic Büro. It is possible to do this with English words: Keks came from cakes a century ago. To do this with more recent words has failed; tränieren never superseded trainieren. When one knows how the loaned word ought to sound in English, it becomes doubly annoying to hear my countrymen muddle the pronunciation.
